analysis.one_liner: Taxes the net wealth of households worth over $50 million, at 2-3% per year.
analysis.headline: A wealth tax on households worth more than $50 million, introduced with 37 cosponsors, sat in the Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would impose a yearly tax on the total net value of what a household owns—assets minus debts—for anyone worth more than $50 million. The rate is 2% on wealth above $50 million and 3% above $1 billion, rising to 6% on billion-dollar fortunes if a Medicare-for-All-style universal health program is ever enacted. It also directs new funding to the IRS to audit at least 30% of those subject to the tax each year and closes reporting loopholes for assets parked abroad.
analysis.who_benefits: Households worth under $50 million—that is, more than 99% of Americans—pay nothing under the bill. The revenue raised from roughly the wealthiest one-tenth of one percent of households would be available for public spending, and the bill specifically authorizes $100 billion over a decade for IRS enforcement, taxpayer services, and systems modernization, which improves service and enforcement for all taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: Households below $50 million in net worth pay a 0% rate; only the ultra-wealthy owe the tax, so more than 99% of taxpayers pay nothing.

The bill requires the IRS to audit at least 30% of taxpayers subject to the wealth tax each year, and authorizes $70 billion for enforcement, $10 billion for taxpayer services, and $20 billion for business systems modernization through fiscal 2034.

The rate on billion-dollar fortunes doubles to 6% in any year a universal, comprehensive health insurance program that bars duplicate private coverage is in effect, tying the tax to funding universal health care.

The bill includes anti-evasion provisions: a 40% tax on covered expatriates' wealth when they renounce citizenship, new reporting rules for assets moved into foreign entities, and a plan to leverage foreign-account data for enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: The roughly 100,000 or fewer households with net worth above $50 million—the top fraction of one percent—would pay 2% to 3% of net wealth per year, and billionaires 3% (6% under universal health coverage). Financial institutions and businesses would face new duties to report asset values to the IRS. Hard-pressed business owners could get up to five years' deferral, but would still owe the tax.

drawbacks.text: Most wealth above $50 million sits in privately held businesses, real estate, and other assets with no market price, so the bill forces the Treasury to build new formulaic valuation rules within 12 months; getting those values wrong is hard to avoid and subject to new 30-50% penalties.

Wealth taxes are hard to collect from mobile fortunes: wealthy households can shift assets abroad, defer realization, or renounce citizenship (though the bill applies a 40% exit tax to covered expatriates), so actual collections may fall short of projections.

A tax on stock and asset holdings—rather than on income or sales—faces unresolved constitutional questions under the Constitution's limits on direct taxes, and litigation could delay or upend collection.

Entrepreneurs whose wealth is tied up in a single operating business could owe a large annual tax without corresponding cash income, though the bill lets the Secretary grant up to five years of payment deferral for severe liquidity constraints or undue hardship.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls entirely on a very small group of very wealthy households, while more than 99% of households pay nothing and stand to benefit from the revenue and from better-funded IRS services. The main honest concerns are practical: valuing private assets is genuinely hard, collection may underperform, and constitutional litigation could stall the tax. These are implementation risks rather than a case that the burden falls on ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and the session ended with no markup and no vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2024 on March 20, 2024, joined by 34 original cosponsors.
All 37 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced, and the record shows no further action—no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote—before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households worth more than $50 million are better off: no annual wealth tax was enacted, and their fortunes remain subject only to the existing income, capital gains, and estate tax rules.

industries.note: The bill would take 2-3% of their net wealth each year, doubling to 6% for billionaires if universal health coverage is enacted. Ordinary households pay a 0% rate, so the burden falls entirely on this group.

industries.industry: Private wealth management and estate planning
industries.note: The tax would create strong demand for valuation shelters and trust structures, and the bill targets exactly those avoidance tools—attribution rules for trusts, a 40% exit tax on expatriates, and expanded foreign-asset reporting.

They would take on new reporting duties, including estimating the value of business entities, to help enforce the tax on the ultra-wealthy. Ordinary taxpayers face no new reporting burden since the exclusion covers small assets.

Fund holdings in billionaires' portfolios are precisely the hard-to-value assets the bill addresses; Treasury could impose formulaic valuations and retrospective adjustment charges. Larger funds and their ultra-wealthy investors bear the cost, not ordinary participants.
